title: ARCO: Adaptive Rubric with Co-Evolution for Multi-Step LLM-Based Agents

paper.title: ARCO: Adaptive Rubric with Co-Evolution for Multi-Step LLM-Based Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning for multi-step LLM agents often relies on scalar rewards that indicate success but cannot explain why a trajectory is good or bad. Rubric-based rewards improve interpretability through natural-language criteria, but existing methods score at the trajectory level and freeze the scorer behind a closed-source judge, leaving step-level credit assignment unresolved and the judge itself static. We propose ARCO ( A daptive R ubric CO -evolution), a rubric framework in which a same-scale model μ \mu shares a backbone with two heads: a generation head that produces per-step criteria, and a score head that predicts rubric-conditioned step-level rewards. A trajectory decomposition constraint ties the sum of step rewards to the terminal outcome, enabling credit assignment without step-level labels, while μ \mu and the policy π \pi are jointly updated on on-policy data so that the rubric content and the scoring function co-evolve at the parameter level. Across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with two open-source backbones, ARCO improves the best EM in every setting over strong outcome-, rubric-, and process-reward baselines, and analyses show that its rubrics are step-specific, robust to design choices, and useful for diagnosing agent behavior. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/zihangtian/ARCO .

Across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with two open-source backbones, ARCO improves the best EM in every setting over strong outcome-, rubric-, and process-reward baselines, and analyses show that its rubrics are step-specific, robust to design choices, and useful for diagnosing agent behavior. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/zihangtian/ARCO . 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard approach for improving multi-step LLM-based agents on tasks such as multi-hop QA and tool use Zeng et al. (2025) ; Kalyan and Andrews (2025) ; Jin et al. (2025) . Most methods train with black-box scalar rewards—either trajectory-level outcome rewards or step-level process rewards—that indicate quality but cannot explain why a trajectory is good or bad Ouyang et al. (2022) ; Lightman et al. (2024) ; Xi et al. (2025) . This opacity invites reward hacking and limits the granularity of credit assignment across steps Gao et al. (2023) . Rubric-based rewards offer a more interpretable alternative by grounding evaluation in explicit natural-language criteria Gunjal et al. (2025) ; Gupta et al. (2025) ; Shao et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025a) . Yet existing rubric methods share two limitations. First, they all operate at the trajectory level: a single rubric scores the entire rollout, leaving the credit-assignment problem at individual steps untouched. Second, they rely on a frozen closed-source LLM (e.g., GPT-4) as the external judge—whether the rubric is static Gunjal et al. (2025) , generated dynamically per trajectory Gupta et al. (2025) , or evolved through an on-policy buffer Shao et al. (2025) , only the rubric text may change while the judge’s parameters never update. Consider a multi-hop question: In what year was the university where Sergei Tokarev was a professor founded? A black-box reward assigns the same score to a trajectory that luckily guesses “1755” and one that methodically searches for Tokarev’s university before looking up its founding year. A static rubric might check “did the agent search?”—but once the agent learns to search, its errors shift to subtler modes: targeting the wrong entity, redundant retrieval, or premature answers. A frozen judge cannot adapt its scoring to these evolving failure modes, regardless of how the rubric text is updated. We argue that an effective reward model for multi-step agents should be (i) rubric-based , providing interpretable criteria rather than opaque scalars; (ii) step-level , assigning per-action scores rather than a single trajectory score; and (iii) co-evolutionary , updating both the evaluation criteria and the scoring function alongside the policy at the parameter level. We propose ARCO ( A daptive R ubric CO -evolution), a self-contained rubric model μ \mu that shares a backbone between a rubric generation head producing per-step natural-language criteria and a score head predicting rubric-conditioned step rewards. Both μ \mu and the policy π \pi are updated jointly on on-policy data, so the evaluation criteria and scoring function co-evolve with the agent’s improving behavior—using the same-scale open-source model, with no external judge. Figure 1: ARCO architecture on a multi-hop QA example. The rubric model μ \mu shares a backbone f θ f_{\theta} with two stages: (1) generate K = 3 K{=}3 natural-language rubric criteria per step, then (2) predict K K dimension scores conditioned on the generated rubric via a score head g ϕ g_{\phi} . The step score s t = mean ⁡ ( d t , 1 , d t , 2 , d t , 3 ) s_{t}=\mathrm{mean}(d_{t,1},d_{t,2},d_{t,3}) , and the decomposition constraint ∑ t s t = R ⁡ ( τ ) \sum_{t}s_{t}=R(\tau) ties step scores to the trajectory outcome. Both μ \mu and π \pi are updated jointly on on-policy data. Our main contributions are: • We introduce ARCO , an adaptive, step-level rubric-based process reward framework in which both the natural-language rubric and the scoring function co-evolve with the policy at the parameter level, removing the dependence on a frozen closed-source judge. • We design a hierarchical rubric model μ \mu with a shared backbone: it generates criteria conditioned on the trajectory prefix and action, then scores the action under those criteria. We use trajectory decomposition to let μ \mu learn from terminal outcomes and co-optimize with the policy. • We conduct extensive experiments demonstrating ARCO’s effectiveness, along with comprehensive analyses that inform future work on interpretable process rewards. 2 Preliminary A multi-step LLM-based agent solves a task q ∈ 𝒬 q\in\mathcal{Q} by sequentially selecting actions a t ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ h t ) a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t}) given a trajectory prefix h t = ( q , a 1 , o 1 , … , a t − 1 , o t − 1 ) h_{t}=(q,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) , producing a trajectory τ \tau with binary reward R ⁡ ( τ ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } R(\tau)\in\{0,1\} . Rubric-based process supervision augments scalar scoring with natural-language criteria: at each step, a generator ρ \rho produces evaluation criteria and a scorer g g predicts a reward conditioned on them: r t = ρ ⁡ ( h t , a t ) , s t = g ⁡ ( h t , a t , r t ) . r_{t}=\rho(h_{t},a_{t}),\qquad s_{t}=g(h_{t},a_{t},r_{t}). (1) Existing methods differ in three design axes. Rubric adaptation : criteria may be static (fixed before training) Gunjal et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025a) , dynamically generated per trajectory but with a frozen generator Gupta et al. (2025) , or evolving at the content level via on-policy buffer management Shao et al. (2025) —yet in all cases the scoring function’s parameters remain frozen, and criteria are typically shared across all steps. Scoring granularity : g g usually produces a single trajectory-level score R ⁡ ( τ ) R(\tau) rather than per-step scores s t s_{t} Gupta et al. (2025) ; Gunjal et al. (2025) . Judge model : existing rubric-based methods rely on closed-source LLMs (e.g. GPT) as external judges, preventing the scorer from co-evolving with the policy. ARCO addresses all three axes: ρ \rho generates context-specific criteria per step using a same-scale model, g g predicts step-level scores conditioned on those criteria, and both ρ \rho and g g are co-evolved with π \pi at the parameter level on on-policy data throughout training. 3 ARCO We consider a multi-step LLM-based agent solving instances q ∈ 𝒬 q\in\mathcal{Q} . At step t t , the policy π \pi observes a trajectory prefix h t = ( q , a 1 , o 1 , … , a t − 1 , o t − 1 ) h_{t}{=}(q,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1},o_{t-1}) and selects an action a t ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ h t ) a_{t}{\sim}\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t}) . The environment returns observations for tool actions such as retrieval, and the trajectory τ \tau receives a binary outcome reward R ⁡ ( τ ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } R(\tau)\in\{0,1\} after the agent finishes or reaches the horizon. ARCO turns this sparse signal into interpretable process supervision by attaching a natural-language rubric r t r_{t} and a scalar score s t s_{t} to every action. Unlike pipelines with a frozen rubric writer or judge, ARCO instantiates both rubric generation and scoring inside one trainable model μ \mu that co-evolves with the policy π \pi . 3.1 Hierarchical Rubric Model The rubric model μ \mu uses one causal LM backbone f θ f_{\theta} with two lightweight heads, separating what should be checked from how well the action satisfies those checks . The hierarchy is motivated by the fact that step quality is structured and operation-dependent: in multi-hop QA, a search may fail by wrong-entity targeting, broad querying, or redundancy, while a finish may fail by missing support or wrong format. A flat scalar PRM must compress these heterogeneous failure modes into one implicit value; ARCO instead writes a local checklist for the current prefix-action pair and scores the action along that checklist, exposing the evaluator’s latent dimensions as readable criteria and narrowing the score head’s prediction problem to a small set of concrete checks. Concretely, the LM head acts as the high-level rubric generator: given ( q , h t , a t ) (q,h_{t},a_{t}) , it generates an ordered rubric r t = ( c t , 1 , … , c t , K ) ∼ p θ ( ⋅ ∣ q , h t , a t ) r_{t}{=}(c_{t,1},\ldots,c_{t,K}){\sim}p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,h_{t},a_{t}) , where each criterion names one aspect of action quality. Because criteria are generated after observing the trajectory prefix, the rubric can adapt across stages: early searches can be judged by entity targeting and evidence coverage, later searches by whether they resolve the remaining hop, and finish actions by answer support and format. The score head acts as the low-level evaluator: it reads the same state-action context together with the generated checklist and converts those semantic checks into numeric supervision. We feed the full scoring sequence ( q , h t , a t , r t ) (q,h_{t},a_{t},r_{t}) through the shared backbone, obtain 𝐡 ¯ t \bar{\mathbf{h}}_{t} by attention-mask mean pooling over non-padding hidden states, and apply the score head g ϕ g_{\phi} to produce K K criterion-level scores, 𝐝 t = g ϕ ​ ( 𝐡 ¯ t ) ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] K , s t = 1 K ​ ∑ j = 1 K d t , j . \mathbf{d}_{t}=g_{\phi}(\bar{\mathbf{h}}_{t})\in[-1,1]^{K},\qquad s_{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}d_{t,j}. (2) Sharing the backbone matters beyond parameter efficiency: with separate models, the writer and scorer would communicate only through generated text and the scorer would have to reinterpret criteria that may drift from its own representation. With shared parameters, the criteria are written in the same representation space used for scoring, and gradients from the decomposition objective shape the features used by both stages—so improvements to one stage transfer to the other through the shared backbone, while the rubric text itself is regularized by the KL term in ℒ μ rl \mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{rl}} (Eq. 5 ). 3.2 Co-Evolutionary Training We perform a supervised warmup before RL: a closed-source LLM teacher (accessed via API) collects trajectories and step rubrics; π \pi is supervised-fine-tuning (SFT) initialized on the trajectories, and μ \mu is initialized by a text-LM loss on the annotated criteria plus a mean-squared error (MSE) on projected criterion scores so that the trajectory-decomposition constraint holds at warmup (Appendix B ).
